chemistry-e1-l1.title: Diverse Properties of Objects and Materials · Basic Inquiry and Core Principles
chemistry-e1-l1.concept: Materials are what objects are made from. Metal, plastic, glass, and rubber each have their own special properties.
chemistry-e1-l1.example: Windows are made of transparent glass that lets light through, and tires are made of rubber that stretches well and is tough.

chemistry-e1-l2.title: Diverse Properties of Objects and Materials · Experiment Analysis and Problem Solving

chemistry-e2-l1.title: Water-Soluble Substances and Mixtures · Basic Inquiry and Core Principles
chemistry-e2-l1.concept: When a substance mixes evenly into a liquid and can no longer be seen, we say it 'dissolves.' Substances that do not dissolve sink to the bottom or float.
chemistry-e2-l1.example: Salt dissolves clearly in water, but sand does not dissolve and sinks to the bottom.

chemistry-e2-l2.title: Water-Soluble Substances and Mixtures · Experiment Analysis and Problem Solving
chemistry-e2-l2.concept: Water-Soluble Substances and Mixtures: builds the ability to interpret experimental data and solve real-life application problems.

chemistry-e3-l1.title: The Three States: Solid, Liquid, and Gas · Basic Inquiry and Core Principles
chemistry-e3-l1.concept: A solid has a fixed shape and volume. A liquid changes shape depending on its container but keeps a fixed volume. A gas freely changes both shape and volume.
chemistry-e3-l1.example: Ice (solid), water (liquid), and water vapor (gas) are the three states of water.

chemistry-e3-l2.title: The Three States: Solid, Liquid, and Gas · Experiment Analysis and Problem Solving
chemistry-e3-l2.concept: The Three States: Solid, Liquid, and Gas: builds the ability to interpret experimental data and solve real-life application problems.
chemistry-e3-l2.example: Draw scientific conclusions through quantitative data analysis and error analysis.

chemistry-e4-l1.title: Evaporation, Boiling, Condensation, and the Volume Change of Ice · Basic Inquiry and Core Principles
chemistry-e4-l1.concept: A liquid turning into a gas is vaporization (evaporation and boiling), a gas turning into a liquid is liquefaction (condensation), and a solid turning into a liquid is melting.
chemistry-e4-l1.example: When water freezes in cold winter, its volume increases and drink cans and plastic bottles bulge.

chemistry-e4-l2.title: Evaporation, Boiling, Condensation, and the Volume Change of Ice · Experiment Analysis and Problem Solving
chemistry-e4-l2.concept: Evaporation, Boiling, Condensation, and the Volume Change of Ice: builds the ability to interpret experimental data and solve real-life application problems.
chemistry-e4-l2.example: Draw scientific conclusions through quantitative data analysis and error analysis.

chemistry-e5-l1.title: Solute, Solvent, Solution, and Concentration · Basic Inquiry and Core Principles
chemistry-e5-l1.concept: The substance that dissolves is the solute, the liquid that dissolves it is the solvent, and the evenly mixed liquid is the solution. Wherever you take a sample from a solution, its taste, color, and concentration are uniform.
chemistry-e5-l1.example: When you dissolve salt (solute) in water (solvent), you get salt water (solution).

chemistry-e5-l2.title: Solute, Solvent, Solution, and Concentration · Experiment Analysis and Problem Solving
chemistry-e5-l2.concept: Solute, Solvent, Solution, and Concentration: builds the ability to interpret experimental data and solve real-life application problems.
chemistry-e5-l2.example: Draw scientific conclusions through quantitative data analysis and error analysis.

chemistry-e6-l1.title: Acidity, Basicity, and the Three Elements of Combustion · Basic Inquiry and Core Principles
chemistry-e6-l1.concept: Acidic solutions (vinegar, lemon juice) turn blue litmus paper red, and basic solutions (soapy water) turn red litmus paper blue. Combustion needs a combustible material, oxygen, and a temperature at or above the ignition point.
chemistry-e6-l1.example: When you add vinegar to red cabbage indicator it turns red, and when you add soapy water it turns blue or yellow.

chemistry-e6-l2.title: Acidity, Basicity, and the Three Elements of Combustion · Experiment Analysis and Problem Solving
chemistry-e6-l2.concept: Acidity, Basicity, and the Three Elements of Combustion: builds the ability to interpret experimental data and solve real-life application problems.
chemistry-e6-l2.example: Draw scientific conclusions through quantitative data analysis and error analysis.

chemistry-m1-l1.title: Boyle's Law, Charles's Law, and Changes of State · Basic Inquiry and Core Principles
chemistry-m1-l1.concept: At constant temperature, the volume of a gas is inversely proportional to its pressure (Boyle's law: $PV=\text{constant}$). At constant pressure, the volume of a gas is proportional to its temperature (Charles's law).
chemistry-m1-l1.example: When you put a dented ping-pong ball into hot water, the gas particles move more actively and the ball pops back out taut.

chemistry-m1-l2.title: Boyle's Law, Charles's Law, and Changes of State · Experiment Analysis and Problem Solving
chemistry-m1-l2.concept: Boyle's Law, Charles's Law, and Changes of State: builds the ability to interpret experimental data and solve real-life application problems.
chemistry-m1-l2.example: Draw scientific conclusions through quantitative data analysis and error analysis.

chemistry-m2-l1.title: Elements, Atoms, Ions, and Precipitation Reactions · Basic Inquiry and Core Principles
chemistry-m2-l1.concept: An element is a basic component of matter. When an atom loses electrons it becomes a cation, and when it gains electrons it becomes an anion. When certain ions meet, they form a precipitate that does not dissolve in water.
chemistry-m2-l1.example: When silver nitrate solution is added to sodium chloride solution, a white silver chloride ($\text{AgCl}$) precipitate forms.

chemistry-m2-l2.title: Elements, Atoms, Ions, and Precipitation Reactions · Experiment Analysis and Problem Solving
chemistry-m2-l2.concept: Elements, Atoms, Ions, and Precipitation Reactions: builds the ability to interpret experimental data and solve real-life application problems.
chemistry-m2-l2.example: Draw scientific conclusions through quantitative data analysis and error analysis.

chemistry-m3-l1.title: Conservation of Mass, Constant Composition, Exothermic and Endothermic Reactions · Basic Inquiry and Core Principles
chemistry-m3-l1.concept: Before and after a chemical reaction, the types and numbers of atoms do not change, so the total mass is conserved. In a compound, the mass ratio between its component elements is constant.
chemistry-m3-l1.example: $1\text{ g}$ of hydrogen and $8\text{ g}$ of oxygen combine to form $9\text{ g}$ of water (mass ratio $1:8$).

chemistry-m3-l2.title: Conservation of Mass, Constant Composition, Exothermic and Endothermic Reactions · Experiment Analysis and Problem Solving
chemistry-m3-l2.concept: Conservation of Mass, Constant Composition, Exothermic and Endothermic Reactions: builds the ability to interpret experimental data and solve real-life application problems.
chemistry-m3-l2.example: Draw scientific conclusions through quantitative data analysis and error analysis.

chemistry-h1-l1.title: Ionic Bonds, Covalent Bonds, and Redox · Basic Inquiry and Core Principles
chemistry-h1-l1.concept: To satisfy the octet rule (the electron configuration of Group 18), elements form ionic or covalent bonds. Oxidation is losing electrons, and reduction is gaining electrons.
chemistry-h1-l1.example: Sodium chloride ($\text{NaCl}$) does not conduct electricity as a solid, but when dissolved in water its ions move and current flows.

chemistry-h1-l2.title: Ionic Bonds, Covalent Bonds, and Redox · Experiment Analysis and Problem Solving
chemistry-h1-l2.concept: Ionic Bonds, Covalent Bonds, and Redox: builds the ability to interpret experimental data and solve real-life application problems.

chemistry-h2-l1.title: The Mole (mol) and Quantitative Relationships in Chemical Equations · Basic Inquiry and Core Principles
chemistry-h2-l1.concept: $6.02 \times 10^{23}$ particles make up $1\text{ mol}$. The ratio of coefficients in a chemical equation equals the ratio of moles, the ratio of numbers of molecules, and the ratio of volumes of gases.
chemistry-h2-l1.example: The volume of $1\text{ mol}$ of gas is $22.4\text{ L}$ at $0^\circ\text{C}$ and $1\text{ atm}$.

chemistry-h2-l2.title: The Mole (mol) and Quantitative Relationships in Chemical Equations · Experiment Analysis and Problem Solving
chemistry-h2-l2.concept: The Mole (mol) and Quantitative Relationships in Chemical Equations: builds the ability to interpret experimental data and solve real-life application problems.

chemistry-h3-l1.title: Reaction Rate, Le Chatelier's Principle, and Galvanic Cells · Basic Inquiry and Core Principles
chemistry-h3-l1.concept: A catalyst controls the rate by changing the activation energy. When a change is applied to a system in dynamic equilibrium, the equilibrium shifts in the direction that relieves that change (Le Chatelier's principle).
chemistry-h3-l1.example: When ammonia is synthesized by the Haber-Bosch process, raising the pressure shifts the equilibrium toward the forward reaction, in which the number of gas molecules decreases.

chemistry-e1-q1.prompt: Which of the following correctly pairs an 'object,' which has a specific shape and a particular use, with the 'material' it is made from?

options.a: Chair (object) — wood (material)
options.b: Glass (object) — cup (material)
options.c: Metal (object) — scissors (material)
options.d: Plastic (object) — dipper (material)

hints: An 'object' is the name of a finished item we use, and a 'material' is the name of what it is made of.
A chair is an item, and wood is the material.
chemistry-e1-q1.explanation: An item with a shape and a use is called an 'object,' and the base substance used to make the object is called a 'material.'

chemistry-e1-q2.prompt: What is the characteristic property of a material that stretches when you pull it, like a rubber band or a balloon, and returns to its original shape when you let go?

options.a: Elasticity
options.b: Transparency
options.c: Magnetism
options.d: Flammability

hints: It is the property of springing back to the original form.
Think of the stretchiness you feel in a rubber band.
chemistry-e1-q2.explanation: The property of an object that has been deformed by an external force returning to its original shape when the force is removed is called 'elasticity.'

chemistry-e1-q3.prompt: Which option correctly pairs the properties of the materials used to make a 'raincoat' worn in the rain and 'swimming goggles' used for water play?

options.a: Raincoat: waterproof, does not let water through / Goggles: transparent, so you can see clearly
options.b: Raincoat: conductive, conducts electricity well / Goggles: brittle, breaks easily
options.c: Raincoat: flammable, burns easily / Goggles: heavy, with great weight
options.d: Raincoat: absorbent, absorbs water well / Goggles: opaque

hints: A raincoat must not let water soak in, and goggles must let you see clearly in front of you.
The use of an item is decided by the properties of its material.
chemistry-e1-q3.explanation: A raincoat is made of a waterproof material (vinyl or plastic) that repels water so it does not get wet in the rain, and swimming goggles are made of transparent plastic or glass to give a clear view underwater.

chemistry-e1-q4.prompt: What is the scientific reason that the body of a frying pan or pot used in the kitchen is made of metal, while the handle is made of plastic or wood?

options.a: Metal conducts heat quickly, while plastic and wood do not conduct heat well, so hands do not get burned
options.b: Because a metal handle would be too light
options.c: Because plastic changes the taste of food for the better
options.d: In order to punch holes in the pot body

hints: To cook food, heat must pass quickly to the bottom of the pot.
If a handle is hot, you cannot hold it.
chemistry-e1-q4.explanation: Metal has high thermal conductivity, so food can be cooked quickly, and plastic and wood are excellent insulators, so you can hold the handle during cooking without being burned.

chemistry-e1-c.prompt: [Advanced Environmental Inquiry] Plastic has the advantages of being light, strong, and non-rotting, but when discarded it does not break down in nature for hundreds of years and pollutes the environment. Which of the following is the correct direction of materials science for solving this problem?

options.a: Developing 'biodegradable plastics,' made from corn starch and similar materials, that are broken down naturally by microorganisms
options.b: Throwing all plastic into the sea to sink it
options.c: Burying plastic deep underground and forgetting about it
options.d: Switching all household goods to single-use only

hints: It is an eco-friendly new material that is nature-friendly and that microorganisms can eat and break down.
It is biodegradable technology.
chemistry-e1-c.explanation: To reduce environmental pollution, biodegradable bioplastics made from plant-based materials, which microorganisms break down into water and carbon dioxide after a certain period of time, are being actively developed.

chemistry-e1-q5.prompt: When a nail or scissors made of iron is exposed to water and air for a long time, it rusts red. Which of the following is a correct materials-science method for preventing this?

options.a: Apply a thin layer of oil or paint it to block contact with air and moisture
options.b: Soak it in water to remove the air
options.c: Wash the iron with salt water every day
options.d: Dry it thoroughly in the sun and keep it hotter

hints: For iron to corrode (oxidize), both oxygen and moisture are needed.
Coating the surface can block oxygen and water.
chemistry-e1-q5.explanation: Corrosion of iron occurs through the interaction of oxygen and moisture, so applying oil, paint, or plating to the surface to completely block contact with air and water prevents rust.

chemistry-e2-q1.prompt: A spoonful of sugar is added to a beaker of warm water and stirred with a glass rod. Which statement correctly describes what happens?

options.a: The sugar grains break into very small pieces and spread evenly throughout the water until they can no longer be seen
options.b: The sugar hardens like a stone at the bottom of the beaker
options.c: The sugar rises above the water and all of it flies off into the air
options.d: The water in the beaker turns black

hints: Observe the phenomenon of dissolving.
It becomes transparent, but if you taste it, it is still sweet.
chemistry-e2-q1.explanation: When sugar dissolves in water, the sugar molecules spread evenly among the water molecules and become invisible, forming clear sugar water.

chemistry-e2-q2.prompt: Why does sugar dissolve much faster in a cup of warm water than in a cup of cold water?

options.a: Because the higher the temperature, the more actively the water molecules move, so they pull the sugar grains apart quickly
options.b: Because warm water cools the sugar down
options.c: Because warm water contains more air
options.d: Because cold water pushes sugar away

hints: The higher the temperature, the faster molecules move.
Think about stirring a sugar cube in a teacup.
chemistry-e2-q2.explanation: The higher the temperature of the water, the more active the thermal motion of the water molecules, so they collide with the sugar particles more often and more strongly, and the dissolving rate increases.

chemistry-e2-q3.prompt: Salt water and muddy water are each poured through a funnel lined with filter paper. Which option correctly pairs what remains on the filter paper?

options.a: Salt water: nothing remains / Muddy water: soil grains are caught on the filter paper
options.b: Salt water: lumps of salt remain / Muddy water: nothing remains
options.c: Both salt water and muddy water pass straight through the filter paper
options.d: Both salt water and muddy water remain entirely on the filter paper

hints: The particles of a fully dissolved solution are much smaller than the holes in the filter paper.
Undissolved soil grains are caught by the filter paper.
chemistry-e2-q3.explanation: Salt dissolves completely, so its particles are much smaller than the gaps in the filter paper and all pass through, but soil grains do not dissolve and cannot pass through the holes in the filter paper, so they remain.

chemistry-e2-q4.prompt: What change of state and separation method is used in a salt field to obtain the clean salt we eat from seawater?

options.a: Using sunlight and wind to evaporate the water from the seawater, leaving only salt crystals
options.b: Boiling seawater vigorously to turn it into ice
options.c: Putting a magnet in seawater to attract the salt
options.d: Straining the seawater through a sieve to pick out only the salt

hints: When seawater spread in a shallow layer in a salt field is exposed to sunlight, only the water becomes water vapor and flies away.
It is a separation of a mixture using evaporation.
chemistry-e2-q4.explanation: When seawater is held in a salt field and the water is evaporated by sunlight and wind, only the water becomes gaseous water vapor and flies away, and only the dissolved salt crystals separate out in white.

chemistry-e2-c.prompt: [Advanced Inquiry into Principles] There is salt water made by completely dissolving 10 g of salt in 100 g of water. How many g will the whole salt water weigh when measured on an electronic balance?
hints: Even though the salt dissolves out of sight, it has not disappeared.
Conservation of mass: (mass of water) + (mass of salt) = ?
chemistry-e2-c.explanation: When a substance dissolves, the particles of the solute (salt) simply scatter among the water molecules and do not disappear, so the weight of the whole solution is exactly conserved at 110 g, the sum of the weights of the water and the salt.

chemistry-e2-q5.prompt: Even if water and cooking oil are put in one bottle and shaken hard, they separate completely into two layers again after sitting still for a moment. Why?

options.a: Because cooking oil does not mix with water and is less dense than water, so it floats on top
options.b: Because the cooking oil absorbs the water
options.c: Because the water is warmer than the cooking oil
options.d: Because the cooking oil has hardened into a solid

hints: Water is polar and oil is nonpolar, so they do not dissolve in each other.
Oil is lighter than water (less dense), so it floats on top.
chemistry-e2-q5.explanation: Water is a polar molecule and cooking oil is a nonpolar molecule, so they do not mix, and the density of cooking oil (about 0.92 g/cm³) is lower than that of water (1.0 g/cm³), so it rises to the upper layer.

chemistry-e3-q1.prompt: Which state of matter freely changes shape depending on its container, but keeps its volume unchanged and constant?

options.a: Liquid
options.b: Solid
options.c: Gas
options.d: Plasma

hints: Think about pouring water or milk into another cup.
The shape follows the cup, but the amount (volume) stays the same.
chemistry-e3-q1.explanation: In a liquid, the bonds between molecules are more flexible than in a solid, so its shape changes easily with the container, but the attraction between molecules is maintained, so its volume is constant.

chemistry-e3-q2.prompt: One syringe is filled with water and another is filled with air. After firmly blocking the opening of each with a finger, the plunger is pushed in hard. What happens?

options.a: The plunger of the air-filled syringe is pushed in a lot, but the plunger of the water-filled syringe barely moves
options.b: The water-filled syringe is pushed in much more than the air-filled one
options.c: Both syringes are pushed in completely to the end
options.d: Neither syringe moves at all

hints: Gas molecules are very far apart from one another, so there is a lot of empty space.
Gases are easily compressed, but liquids are very hard to compress.
chemistry-e3-q2.explanation: In a gas (air), the distance between molecules is very large, so when pressure is applied it is easily compressed and its volume decreases, but in a liquid (water), the molecules are already packed closely together, so it is hardly compressed.

chemistry-e3-q3.prompt: Which of the following is a characteristic common to the 'solid' materials we commonly see around us?

options.a: Shape and volume stay constant even when the container changes
options.b: Shape changes freely depending on the container
options.c: It cannot be held in the hand and cannot be seen at all
options.d: It fills the whole space and spreads out endlessly

hints: Think about moving a block of wood or a pebble into another box.
The shape does not change.
chemistry-e3-q3.explanation: In a solid, the particles that make up the matter are firmly bound in a regular arrangement, so shape and volume stay constant unless an external force is applied.

chemistry-e3-q4.prompt: When a perfume bottle was opened in one corner of a room, after a while the faint fragrance reached the nose of a person on the opposite side of the room. What is the scientific principle that explains this phenomenon?

options.a: The phenomenon of 'diffusion,' in which perfume gas particles move on their own and spread through the air
options.b: Because the liquid perfume froze and rolled across the floor
options.c: Because the perfume molecules pulled the nose toward them like a magnet
options.d: Because the air ate up the smell of the perfume

hints: The particles that make up matter do not stay still but keep moving on their own constantly.
What is the phenomenon of gas spreading out called?
chemistry-e3-q4.explanation: The phenomenon in which perfume particles in the air keep moving freely in all directions on their own and spread from places of high concentration to places of low concentration is called 'diffusion.'

chemistry-e3-c.prompt: [Advanced Thought Experiment] Does air, which cannot be seen, also have weight (mass), like a solid or a liquid? What is the most valid experimental method to prove this?

options.a: Weigh a basketball filled with air on a precision electronic balance, then let the air out, weigh it again, and check the difference in weight
options.b: Throw a balloon high and watch it fly
options.c: Leave an empty glass bottle in the sun and check whether it gets warm
options.d: Put a hand in water and measure how cold the water is

hints: A gas is also matter, so it has mass.
Compare the balance readings with the air in and with the air out.
chemistry-e3-c.explanation: If you measure the weight of a ball filled tightly with air, then let the air out and measure again, you can confirm that the weight decreases, and this proves that air, a gas, also has mass and weight.

chemistry-e3-q5.prompt: When cold 'dry ice,' put in with ice cream packaging, is left at room temperature, no liquid droplets form at all, and it goes straight into a gas and disappears. What is this change of state?

options.a: 'Sublimation,' in which a solid changes directly into a gas without passing through a liquid
options.b: 'Melting,' in which a solid melts into a liquid
options.c: 'Vaporization,' in which a liquid boils into a gas
options.d: 'Liquefaction,' in which a gas changes into a liquid

hints: Dry ice is solid carbon dioxide.
At room temperature and 1 atm, it sublimes directly into a gas without passing through the liquid state.
chemistry-e3-q5.explanation: Dry ice (solid carbon dioxide) cannot exist as a liquid at normal pressure (1 atm) and shows 'sublimation' (vaporization by sublimation), changing from a solid directly into a gas.

chemistry-e4-q1.prompt: A cold drink can just taken out of the refrigerator was left on the table for a while, and droplets of water formed on the surface of the can. Where did these droplets come from?

options.a: Water vapor, a gas in the air, touched the cold can and condensed into liquid water
options.b: The drink leaked out through the aluminum wall of the can
options.c: Droplets formed from the paint on the can surface melting
options.d: Sap squeezed out of the wood of the table

hints: Invisible water vapor is always floating in the air.
When water vapor meets a cold surface, it cools and turns into liquid droplets (condensation).
chemistry-e4-q1.explanation: This is 'condensation (liquefaction),' in which water vapor in the air, in a gaseous state, meets the cold surface of the can, loses heat, and changes into liquid water droplets.

chemistry-e4-q2.prompt: Which statement correctly describes the changes in weight and volume when liquid water freezes into solid ice?

options.a: The weight stays the same, but the volume increases
options.b: Both weight and volume decrease
options.c: The weight increases, but the volume decreases
options.d: Both weight and volume increase

hints: Even when water freezes, the total number of molecules that make up the matter does not change.
When ice forms, it takes on a hexagonal ring structure and the empty space grows.
chemistry-e4-q2.explanation: When water freezes into ice, mass (weight) is conserved, but because the water molecules form hexagonal crystals with a lot of empty space through hydrogen bonds, the volume increases by about 10%.

chemistry-e4-q3.prompt: What is the fundamental scientific cause of 'freeze-bursting accidents,' in which outdoor water pipes freeze and burst in the severe sub-zero cold of winter?

options.a: Because the water in the pipe expands in volume as it freezes and pushes hard against the pipe wall
options.b: Because the iron pipe shrinks in the cold and melts away
options.c: Because water pressure suddenly rises tenfold in winter
options.d: Because ice generates electricity and burns the pipe

hints: Think about how the volume changes when water changes state into ice.
When water freezes, its volume increases.
chemistry-e4-q3.explanation: Water has the unusual property of expanding in volume as it freezes, so when the water inside a pipe that is full freezes, the expansion pressure causes freeze-bursting that breaks even a sturdy metal pipe.

chemistry-e4-q4.prompt: Which statement correctly explains the difference between 'evaporation' and 'boiling' that occur when water is heated in a pot?

options.a: Evaporation occurs only at the surface of a liquid, while boiling occurs at the boiling point (100℃) with bubbles forming at the surface and throughout the interior of the liquid
options.b: Evaporation occurs only at 100℃, and boiling occurs at all temperatures
options.c: Evaporation is water turning into ice, and boiling is water turning into water vapor
options.d: Evaporation and boiling are exactly the same phenomenon

hints: Laundry drying is evaporation, which happens slowly at the surface even at low temperatures.
Water boiling vigorously is boiling, with bubbles bursting from inside at 100 degrees.
chemistry-e4-q4.explanation: Evaporation is the phenomenon in which molecules at the liquid surface vaporize even at temperatures below the boiling point, and boiling is the phenomenon in which, on reaching the boiling point, vaporization occurs actively not only at the surface but throughout the interior of the liquid.

chemistry-e4-c.prompt: [Advanced Change of State] Water in a beaker was heated until it began to boil vigorously. Why does the thermometer reading stop rising above 100℃ even if the flame is made stronger and heat continues to be applied?

options.a: Because the supplied heat energy is used entirely for the change of state of water into water vapor (heat of vaporization) instead of raising the temperature of the water
options.b: Because the thermometer breaks above 100 degrees
options.c: Because the water can no longer absorb heat
options.d: Because the water vapor cools the thermometer

hints: While matter changes state, its temperature stays constant.
This is called 'latent heat (heat of vaporization).'
chemistry-e4-c.explanation: While a pure liquid boils, the heat energy applied is used up entirely in breaking the attractions between molecules and converting them to the gaseous state (heat of vaporization), so the temperature stays constant until all of the water has turned into water vapor.

chemistry-e4-q5.prompt: Which option correctly pairs the change-of-state processes of the clear 'dew' that forms on blades of grass in the early morning and the white 'frost' that forms on windows and roofs on late-autumn nights?

options.a: Dew: water vapor turns into liquid droplets (liquefaction) / Frost: water vapor turns directly into ice crystals (sublimation)
options.b: Dew: ice melts (melting) / Frost: water boils (vaporization)
options.c: Both dew and frost are water that evaporated into water vapor
options.d: Dew: spring water that welled up from the ground / Frost: snow that fell from the sky

hints: Dew is liquid water droplets (water vapor → liquid).
Frost is ice crystals that form at sub-zero temperatures (water vapor → solid).
chemistry-e4-q5.explanation: Dew is water vapor in the air condensing (liquefying) on the surface of grass blades chilled overnight, and frost is deposition (solidifying sublimation), in which water vapor at sub-zero temperatures turns directly into ice crystals without passing through a liquid.

chemistry-e5-q1.prompt: 200 g of water has 50 g of sugar added and completely dissolved. In this sugar water, which option correctly pairs the 'solvent,' 'solute,' and 'solution'?

options.a: Solvent: water / Solute: sugar / Solution: sugar water
options.b: Solvent: sugar / Solute: water / Solution: sugar water
options.c: Solvent: sugar water / Solute: sugar / Solution: water
options.d: Solvent: water / Solute: sugar water / Solution: sugar

hints: The liquid that dissolves = solvent, the substance that dissolves = solute, the finished mixture = solution.
In sugar water, the sugar that dissolves is the solute and the water that dissolves it is the solvent.
chemistry-e5-q1.explanation: Water, the substance that dissolves things, is the 'solvent,' sugar, which dissolves, is the 'solute,' and the clear mixture in which the two are evenly mixed is called the 'solution.'

chemistry-e5-q2.prompt: You want to investigate the properties of a salt water solution in a beaker. Which statement correctly describes a characteristic of a solution, which is a homogeneous mixture?

options.a: Whether you take a sample from the top, middle, or bottom of the solution, the degree of saltiness (concentration) is perfectly identical
options.b: Over time, the salt is heavy and settles to the bottom on its own
options.c: Under a magnifying glass, you can see grains of salt floating in the water
options.d: When filtered through filter paper, all of the salt is caught on the filter paper

hints: A solution is a 'homogeneous mixture' in which the particles are evenly mixed at the molecular level.
It does not settle no matter how long you leave it.
chemistry-e5-q2.explanation: In a true solution (a homogeneous mixture), the solute particles are uniformly dispersed among the solvent molecules, so it does not settle even after standing for a long time, and the concentration is the same at every position.

chemistry-e5-q3.prompt: When salt is added to 100 g of water, why does more salt dissolve when the water temperature is 60℃ than when it is 20℃?

options.a: Because the higher the temperature, the more active the thermal motion of the solvent molecules and the greater the solubility, the amount of solute that can be accommodated
options.b: Because high temperature destroys the molecular structure of salt
options.c: Because warm water evaporates the salt
options.d: Because salt likes cold water

hints: Recall the curve of solubility change with temperature.
The warmer it is, the more active the molecular motion of the matter.
chemistry-e5-q3.explanation: For most solid solutes, as the temperature rises, the motion of the solvent particles becomes more active and, owing to the enthalpy conditions of the dissolving process, the solubility (the maximum amount that can dissolve in a given amount of solvent) increases.

chemistry-e5-q4.prompt: A cherry tomato was put in a tank of plain water and sank to the bottom. After a generous amount of salt was added to the tank and stirred, the cherry tomato floated up to the surface. Why?

options.a: Because the salt dissolved and the density of the salt water solution became greater than the density of the cherry tomato
options.b: Because the salt lightly gnawed away at the cherry tomato
options.c: Because the cherry tomato got cold and gave off air
options.d: Because the salt water conducted electricity

hints: If the density of a liquid is greater than the density of an object, the object floats up.
The more salt dissolves, the greater the weight (density) of the liquid.
chemistry-e5-q4.explanation: Salt water is denser than plain water, and when salt keeps dissolving until the density of the salt water becomes greater than the average density of the cherry tomato, the buoyant force becomes greater than gravity and the tomato floats up.

chemistry-e5-c.prompt: [Advanced Crystallization] A saturated solution was made by dissolving alum in warm water at 60℃ until no more would dissolve, a silk thread was hung in this solution, and it was slowly cooled at room temperature, and beautiful gem-shaped alum crystals grew on the silk thread. What is the principle behind this phenomenon?

options.a: Because as the temperature falls, the solubility of alum decreases, and the amount that can no longer stay dissolved separates out as solid crystals
options.b: Because the alum solution froze into ice
options.c: Because the silk thread chemically synthesized alum
options.d: Because dust in the air turned into alum

hints: What happens when a solid that was dissolved in large amounts while warm cools down?
When the temperature drops and the solubility becomes smaller, it is pushed out (precipitation).
chemistry-e5-c.explanation: When the temperature falls, the solubility of a solid decreases sharply, so the supersaturated solute that was dissolved in an amount greater than the lowered solubility joins together into regular crystals and comes out, which is the phenomenon of 'recrystallization (precipitation).'

chemistry-e5-q5.prompt: What is the scientific principle by which, when you open the lid of a can of a cold carbonated drink (cider or cola), there is a 'psst' sound and bubbles actively rise in the drink?

options.a: Because when the can is opened, the internal pressure drops to atmospheric pressure, and the solubility of carbon dioxide gas decreases sharply
options.b: Because when the can is opened, the temperature of the drink suddenly drops below zero
options.c: Because the water in the drink evaporates instantly
options.d: Because oxygen in the air is sucked into the drink

hints: Think about Henry's law.
The solubility of a gas increases at higher pressure and decreases when the pressure drops.
chemistry-e5-q5.explanation: The carbon dioxide gas that was dissolved in large amounts in the water under the high pressure inside the sealed can comes out as bubbles, because when the lid is opened and the pressure drops, its solubility decreases according to Henry's law.

chemistry-e6-q1.prompt: Several solutions were dropped onto red cabbage indicator: solution A turned red, and solution B turned blue and then yellow. Which is correct about the properties of the two solutions?

options.a: Solution A is acidic, solution B is basic
options.b: Solution A is basic, solution B is acidic
options.c: Solutions A and B are both neutral
options.d: Solution A is neutral, solution B is acidic

hints: Red cabbage juice, a natural indicator, contains anthocyanin pigments.
It changes to reddish colors in acid, and to bluish-to-yellowish colors in base.
chemistry-e6-q1.explanation: Red cabbage indicator changes to reddish colors in acidic solutions, and to blue, green, and yellow colors in basic solutions.

chemistry-e6-q2.prompt: When dilute hydrochloric acid or vinegar was dropped onto eggshell or a piece of marble (containing calcium carbonate), bubbles fizzed up. What change occurs when this gas is collected and passed through limewater?

options.a: The limewater turns cloudy white (confirming carbon dioxide gas)
options.b: When a flame is held to the limewater, it burns with a pop
options.c: The color of the limewater turns blue
options.d: No change occurs at all

hints: When a carbonate reacts with an acid, carbon dioxide (CO₂) gas is produced.
When carbon dioxide is passed through limewater, a calcium carbonate precipitate forms and makes it cloudy.
chemistry-e6-q2.explanation: When calcium carbonate ($\text{CaCO}_3$) reacts with an acid, carbon dioxide ($\text{CO}_2$) gas is produced, and the carbon dioxide reacts with limewater ($\text{Ca(OH)}_2$) to form a white calcium carbonate precipitate, making it turn cloudy.

chemistry-e6-q3.prompt: What is the scientific principle behind the household wisdom of sprinkling lemon juice or vinegar when cooking fish in order to get rid of the fishy smell (trimethylamine and similar compounds, which are basic)?

options.a: Because an acidic substance (lemon juice) meets the basic fishy-smelling substances and causes a neutralization reaction
options.b: Because lemon juice freezes the fish flesh
options.c: Because vinegar dissolves and removes the calcium in the fish bones
options.d: Because the yellow color of the lemon covers up the smell

hints: When an acid and a base meet, a 'neutralization reaction' occurs in which each loses its properties.
The fishy-smelling compounds are basic.
chemistry-e6-q3.explanation: Amines, the cause of the fishy smell of fish, are basic, so when an acidic substance such as lemon juice (citric acid) or vinegar (acetic acid) is sprinkled on, an acid-base neutralization reaction occurs and the fishy smell disappears.

chemistry-e6-q4.prompt: After a campfire at a campsite, covering it with soil or sand or spraying it with a fire extinguisher to put it out blocks which of the 'three elements of combustion'?

options.a: Cutting off the supply of oxygen in the air (smothering)
options.b: Completely removing the combustible material (firewood) itself
options.c: Raising the temperature above the ignition point
options.d: Absorbing the surrounding carbon dioxide

hints: The three elements of combustion: combustible material, oxygen, and a temperature at or above the ignition point
If you cover it with sand, air cannot reach the flame.
chemistry-e6-q4.explanation: Covering a fire with sand or a thick blanket, or spraying it with a carbon dioxide extinguisher, puts out the fire by completely cutting off the inflow of oxygen, which is the 'smothering' method.

chemistry-e6-c.prompt: [Advanced Reaction Reasoning] Dilute hydrochloric acid was added little by little with a dropper to a sodium hydroxide solution, which turns red litmus paper blue, and mixed. Which describes the change that occurs in the mixed solution when a sufficient amount of hydrochloric acid has been added?

options.a: Heat is released and the temperature rises, and the final solution turns blue litmus paper red
options.b: The solution suddenly becomes cold and turns into ice
options.c: No reaction occurs at all and it stays as it was
options.d: Only hydrogen gas is produced explosively

hints: In a neutralization reaction, heat of neutralization is released and the temperature rises.
If hydrochloric acid is added in excess, it becomes an acidic solution.
chemistry-e6-c.explanation: When an acid (hydrochloric acid) and a base (sodium hydroxide) react, water and a salt are produced and heat of neutralization is released, so the temperature rises. If hydrochloric acid is added in excess, the entire solution becomes acidic and turns blue litmus paper red.

chemistry-e6-q5.prompt: When a large forest fire is spreading, cutting down the trees ahead of the fire's path widely with chainsaws in advance to build a 'firebreak' removes which of the three elements of combustion?

options.a: Removing the combustible material (fuel)
options.b: Blocking oxygen
options.c: Lowering the temperature below the ignition point
options.d: Supplying carbon dioxide

hints: For a fire to keep burning, combustible material must stay continuously connected.
If the trees are removed in advance, the fire has nowhere left to spread.
chemistry-e6-q5.explanation: This is the removal method of fire suppression, which stops a forest fire from spreading by removing in advance the 'combustible material,' one of the essential elements of combustion, so that there is no fuel to burn in the path the flames are advancing along.

chemistry-m1-q1.prompt: What is the fundamental cause of the 'gas pressure' felt on the walls of a sealed container holding a gas?

options.a: Because a huge number of gas particles, constantly moving on their own, collide with the walls of the container
options.b: Because gas particles only sink to the bottom due to Earth's gravity
options.c: Because gas particles attract one another electrostatically
options.d: Because gas particles try to dissolve the container wall away

hints: Gas molecules fly around at very high speeds.
The number and strength of collisions with the wall create pressure.
chemistry-m1-q1.explanation: Gas pressure arises from the force per unit area exerted when gas particles, moving constantly and randomly, collide with the inner wall of the container.

chemistry-m1-q2.prompt: At constant temperature, the pressure of a gas with a volume of 60 mL at 1 atm was raised to 3 atm. According to Boyle's law, what is the volume of this gas?

options.a: 20 mL
options.b: 180 mL
options.c: 30 mL
options.d: 120 mL

hints: Boyle's law: P₁V₁ = P₂V₂
1 atm × 60 mL = 3 atm × (?) mL
chemistry-m1-q2.explanation: According to Boyle's law, $P_1 V_1 = P_2 V_2$ holds at constant temperature. $1\text{ atm} \times 60\text{ mL} = 3\text{ atm} \times V_2 \implies V_2 = 20\text{ mL}$.

chemistry-m1-q3.prompt: When a bag of snacks was carried up a high mountain, the snack bag swelled up tightly, as if about to burst. Which option explains the reason in terms of the relationship between gas pressure and volume?

options.a: Because the higher you go up the mountain, the lower the atmospheric pressure (external pressure) becomes, so the volume of the gas inside the snack bag expanded
options.b: Because the temperature on the mountain was too high and the gas expanded
options.c: Because the snacks in the bag evaporated
options.d: Because oxygen on the mountain seeped into the snack bag

hints: At higher altitude, the air thins and atmospheric pressure decreases.
When the external pressure becomes smaller, the volume of the gas increases (Boyle's law).
chemistry-m1-q3.explanation: As altitude increases, atmospheric pressure decreases. The pressure of the gas inside the bag becomes greater than the outside atmospheric pressure, so the volume of the gas inside expands until the inside and outside pressures become equal.

chemistry-m1-q4.prompt: A dented ping-pong ball was put into hot water, and the ping-pong ball popped back out round and taut. Which is the correct explanation using Charles's law and the particle model of gases?

options.a: Because the temperature rose, the gas particles inside the ping-pong ball moved more actively, the number and strength of collisions increased, and the volume expanded
options.b: Because the plastic of the ping-pong ball absorbed water and became thicker
options.c: Because hot water seeped into the ping-pong ball and filled it
options.d: Because the temperature rose and the number of gas molecules inside the ping-pong ball doubled

hints: Charles's law: at constant pressure, when the temperature rises, the volume of a gas expands.
When the temperature rises, the average speed of gas particles increases.
chemistry-m1-q4.explanation: According to Charles's law, when the temperature rises, the average kinetic energy of the gas molecules increases and their collisions with the inner wall become stronger, so the internal pressure increases and the dented ball pops back out.

chemistry-m1-c.prompt: [Advanced Diffusion Rate] Cotton soaked in concentrated ammonia water (molecular mass 17) and cotton soaked in concentrated hydrochloric acid (molecular mass 36.5) were placed at the same time at the two ends of a long glass tube and the ends were plugged with rubber stoppers. After a while, a band of white smoke (ammonium chloride) formed inside the glass tube. Where is it located, closer to which end?

options.a: Closer to the cotton soaked in hydrochloric acid
options.b: Closer to the cotton soaked in ammonia water
options.c: Exactly in the middle of the glass tube
options.d: In the air outside the glass tube

hints: The lighter the gas molecules, the faster they diffuse (Graham's law of diffusion).
Ammonia (17) is much lighter than hydrogen chloride (36.5).
chemistry-m1-c.explanation: The diffusion rate of a gas is inversely proportional to the square root of its molecular mass. Ammonia gas, which is light with a molecular mass of 17, travels much faster than the heavier hydrogen chloride gas (36.5), so the two gases meet and react at a position closer to the hydrochloric acid cotton, where the relatively slower hydrogen chloride has moved less, forming the white smoke band.

chemistry-m1-q5.prompt: A taut rubber balloon filled with air was placed in liquid nitrogen at -196℃, and it lost almost all of its volume and shrank flat. Which is the correct reason?

options.a: At extremely low temperature the kinetic energy of the gas molecules in the balloon becomes extremely sluggish, so the distance between molecules decreases
options.b: The balloon rubber let all the gas pass out
options.c: All the air inside the balloon was destroyed and disappeared
options.d: The liquid nitrogen pierced the balloon sharply

hints: Charles's law: the volume of a gas is proportional to its absolute temperature.
When the temperature gets very low, gas molecules slow down almost to a standstill.
chemistry-m1-q5.explanation: According to Charles's law, when the temperature is cooled rapidly to $196^\circ\text{C}$ below zero, the thermal motion of the gas molecules slows markedly and some of the gas liquefies, so the internal volume shrinks dramatically.

chemistry-m2-q1.prompt: What is the fundamental reason an atom, made of a nucleus and electrons, is electrically neutral?

options.a: The positive (+) charge of the nucleus and the total negative (-) charge of the electrons orbiting it are equal in magnitude
options.b: There are no neutrons in the nucleus
options.c: Electrons have no charge at all
options.d: Atoms are too small to carry an electric charge

hints: The nucleus is positively (+) charged because of its protons.
Electrons are negatively (-) charged.
chemistry-m2-q1.explanation: An atom is electrically neutral because the total positive (+) charge of the protons in the central nucleus is exactly equal in magnitude to the total negative (-) charge of the electrons in orbit.

chemistry-m2-q2.prompt: Which statement about the formation of an 'ion', when a neutral atom loses or gains electrons and becomes charged, is correct?

options.a: Metal atoms tend to lose electrons and become positive (+) ions, and nonmetal atoms tend to gain electrons and become negative (-) ions
options.b: Protons from the nucleus pop out and form an anion
options.c: Losing electrons produces a negatively (-) charged anion
options.d: The total number of electrons does not change when an ion forms

hints: Sodium (Na) loses 1 electron and becomes Na⁺.
Chlorine (Cl) gains 1 electron and becomes Cl⁻.
chemistry-m2-q2.explanation: An atom either loses electrons from its outermost shell to become a cation (mostly metals), or gains electrons to form an anion that satisfies the octet rule (mostly nonmetals).

chemistry-m2-q3.prompt: Unknown samples A and B were placed in the outer flame; sample A gave a yellow flame color and sample B gave a blue-green flame color. Which metal elements do samples A and B contain, respectively?

options.a: Sample A: sodium (Na) / Sample B: copper (Cu)
options.b: Sample A: potassium (K) / Sample B: strontium (Sr)
options.c: Sample A: copper (Cu) / Sample B: lithium (Li)
options.d: Sample A: barium (Ba) / Sample B: sodium (Na)

hints: The flame color of sodium in salt is bright yellow.
Copper shows its characteristic blue-green flame.
chemistry-m2-q3.explanation: Each metal element shows its own characteristic flame color. Sodium ($\text{Na}$) gives a yellow flame and copper ($\text{Cu}$) gives a blue-green flame.

chemistry-m2-q4.prompt: To check whether chloride ions (Cl⁻), left in tap water as a disinfection by-product, are present, which reagent should be added, and what is the chemical formula of the white precipitate formed?

options.a: Silver nitrate (AgNO₃) solution — silver chloride (AgCl)
options.b: Sodium hydroxide (NaOH) solution — silver hydroxide (AgOH)
options.c: Barium chloride (BaCl₂) solution — barium sulfate (BaSO₄)
options.d: Phenolphthalein solution — silver carbonate (Ag₂CO₃)

hints: When silver ions (Ag⁺) meet chloride ions (Cl⁻), a white precipitate that does not dissolve in water forms.
Precipitation reaction equation: Ag⁺ + Cl⁻ → AgCl↓
chemistry-m2-q4.explanation: When the silver ions ($\text{Ag}^+$) in silver nitrate solution react with the chloride ions ($\text{Cl}^-$) in the water, they form a white silver chloride ($\text{AgCl}$) precipitate that does not dissolve in water, so chloride ions can be detected.

chemistry-m2-c.prompt: [Advanced ion analysis] You want to check whether lead ions (Pb²⁺) are present in factory wastewater. When potassium iodide (KI) solution is added, which is the correct color and chemical formula of the precipitate that appears?

options.a: Yellow precipitate — lead(II) iodide (PbI₂)
options.b: Black precipitate — lead oxide (PbO)
options.c: White precipitate — lead(II) chloride (PbCl₂)
options.d: Blue precipitate — lead(II) nitrate (Pb(NO₃)₂)

hints: When lead ions meet iodide ions, a vivid yellow precipitate forms.
Pb²⁺ + 2I⁻ → PbI₂↓
chemistry-m2-c.explanation: When lead ions ($\text{Pb}^{2+}$) react with iodide ions ($\text{I}^-$), a distinctive, vivid yellow precipitate, lead(II) iodide ($\text{PbI}_2$), forms.

chemistry-m2-q5.prompt: When water is electrolyzed with a small amount of electrolyte added, which choice correctly pairs the gases produced at the (-) electrode and the (+) electrode with their volume ratio?

options.a: (-) electrode: hydrogen (H₂),  (+) electrode: oxygen (O₂),  volume ratio = 2 : 1
options.b: (-) electrode: oxygen (O₂),  (+) electrode: hydrogen (H₂),  volume ratio = 1 : 2
options.c: (-) electrode: hydrogen (H₂),  (+) electrode: chlorine (Cl₂),  volume ratio = 1 : 1
options.d: (-) electrode: water vapor,  (+) electrode: nitrogen,  volume ratio = 2 : 1

hints: The chemical formula of water is H₂O (2 hydrogen atoms and 1 oxygen atom).
Electrolysis equation: 2H₂O → 2H₂ + O₂
chemistry-m2-q5.explanation: According to the electrolysis equation of water, $2\text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightarrow 2\text{H}_2(g) + \text{O}_2(g)$, hydrogen gas is produced at the (-) electrode, where reduction occurs, in a volume of $2$, and oxygen gas is produced at the (+) electrode, where oxidation occurs, in a volume of $1$.

chemistry-m3-q1.prompt: What is the fundamental reason the 'law of conservation of mass' holds when a chemical change occurs?

options.a: The kinds and numbers of atoms that make up the substances never change before and after the reaction
options.b: The total number of molecules is always constant
options.c: New atoms arise on their own
options.d: No heat is produced when a chemical reaction occurs

hints: Recall Lavoisier's law of conservation of mass.
Atoms are only rearranged; they are never created or destroyed.
chemistry-m3-q1.explanation: In a chemical reaction, the way atoms are bonded changes and new substances form, but the kinds and numbers of atoms are neither created nor destroyed and are conserved as they were, so the total mass does not change.

chemistry-m3-q2.prompt: An experiment was done in which copper powder was heated in air in a crucible to make copper(II) oxide. When 4 g of copper reacted completely, 5 g of copper(II) oxide was produced. What is the mass of oxygen that combined, and what is the mass ratio of copper to oxygen?

options.a: Oxygen 1 g,  copper : oxygen = 4 : 1
options.b: Oxygen 2 g,  copper : oxygen = 2 : 1
options.c: Oxygen 5 g,  copper : oxygen = 4 : 5
options.d: Oxygen 0.5 g,  copper : oxygen = 8 : 1

hints: Law of conservation of mass: (copper 4 g) + (oxygen ? g) = copper(II) oxide 5 g
Law of definite proportions: simplify the mass ratio of copper to oxygen.
chemistry-m3-q2.explanation: The mass of oxygen that reacted is $5\text{ g} - 4\text{ g} = 1\text{ g}$. By the law of definite proportions, the mass ratio of copper to oxygen in copper(II) oxide is always $4 : 1$.

chemistry-m3-q3.prompt: At the same temperature and pressure, hydrogen gas and oxygen gas react to produce water vapor. Which is the correct 'volume ratio' of the hydrogen and oxygen that react and the water vapor produced? (law of combining volumes of gases)

options.a: Hydrogen : oxygen : water vapor = 2 : 1 : 2
options.b: Hydrogen : oxygen : water vapor = 1 : 1 : 1
options.c: Hydrogen : oxygen : water vapor = 2 : 1 : 3
options.d: Hydrogen : oxygen : water vapor = 1 : 2 : 2

hints: Chemical equation: 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(g)
By Avogadro's law, for gases the ratio of coefficients = ratio of moles = ratio of volumes.
chemistry-m3-q3.explanation: In the chemical equation $2\text{H}_2(g) + \text{O}_2(g) \rightarrow 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(g)$, at the same temperature and pressure the ratio of gas coefficients equals both the ratio of molecules and the ratio of volumes, so it is $2 : 1 : 2$.

chemistry-m3-q4.prompt: Which choice correctly pairs the energy flow of the shake-to-activate portable hand warmer used in winter (oxidation of iron powder) and the cold pack used to treat acute sprains (reaction of ammonium nitrate with water)?

options.a: Hand warmer: exothermic reaction that releases heat / Cold pack: endothermic reaction that absorbs heat
options.b: Hand warmer: endothermic reaction that absorbs heat / Cold pack: exothermic reaction that releases heat
options.c: Both the hand warmer and the cold pack are exothermic reactions
options.d: Neither the hand warmer nor the cold pack has any energy flow

hints: A hand warmer warms its surroundings, so it releases heat (exothermic).
A cold pack takes heat from its surroundings and makes them cold, so it absorbs heat (endothermic).
chemistry-m3-q4.explanation: The oxidation of iron is an exothermic reaction that releases heat energy to the surroundings and raises the temperature, whereas the dissolving of ammonium nitrate is an endothermic reaction that absorbs heat energy from the surroundings and lowers the temperature.

chemistry-m3-c.prompt: [Advanced reaction coefficients] When propane gas (C₃H₈) burns completely with oxygen (O₂), carbon dioxide (CO₂) and water (H₂O) are produced. In the balanced chemical equation C₃H₈ + a O₂ → b CO₂ + c H₂O, what is the sum of the coefficients (a, b, c), that is, a + b + c?
hints: Number of C atoms: b = 3
Number of H atoms: 2c = 8 → c = 4. Number of O atoms: 2a = 2b + c = 6 + 4 = 10 → a = 5. a + b + c = 5 + 3 + 4 = ?
chemistry-m3-c.explanation: The balanced chemical equation is $\text{C}_3\text{H}_8 + 5\text{O}_2 \rightarrow 3\text{CO}_2 + 4\text{H}_2\text{O}$. So the coefficients are $a=5, b=3, c=4$, and their sum is $5 + 3 + 4 = 12$.

chemistry-m3-q5.prompt: Hydrogen peroxide solution (H₂O₂) decomposes into water and oxygen very slowly at room temperature. When a small amount of black manganese dioxide (MnO₂) powder was added, bubbles (oxygen gas) were produced explosively. What is the role of manganese dioxide?

options.a: A 'catalyst' that does not itself react or get used up and only speeds up the reaction
options.b: A reactant that combines with hydrogen peroxide to become a new compound
options.c: An absorbent that absorbs all the oxygen produced
options.d: An oxidizing agent that makes the solution acidic

hints: The mass and properties of manganese dioxide do not change at all before and after the reaction.
It is a helper that adjusts the reaction rate to be faster.

chemistry-h1-q1.prompt: Which is the most accurate result of an experiment comparing the electrical conductivity of substance A (sodium chloride) and substance B (sugar)?

chemistry-h1-q3.prompt: Which is the correct definition of 'oxidation' and 'reduction' in modern chemistry, based on the transfer of electrons?

chemistry-h1-q4.prompt: What is the principle of 'cathodic protection (sacrificial anode method)', in which lumps of zinc (Zn) or magnesium (Mg) are attached to bridges or ships made of iron (Fe) to prevent them from rusting?

chemistry-h2-q1.prompt: At 0℃ and 1 atm, how many moles of methane molecules, and how many total moles of hydrogen (H) atoms, are in 11.2 L of methane gas (CH₄, molecular mass 16)?

chemistry-killer-01.prompt:
Copper (Cu) powder is heated with oxygen ($\mathrm{O_2}$) in a closed container to form copper(II) oxide ($\mathrm{CuO}$). In every experiment the container holds 2.0 g of $\mathrm{O_2}$, and the reaction is $\mathrm{2Cu + O_2 \rightarrow 2CuO}$. The masses of CuO formed are:
(A) Cu 4.0 g -> CuO 5.0 g
(B) Cu 8.0 g -> CuO 10.0 g
(C) Cu 12.0 g -> CuO 10.0 g
The law of definite proportions holds under the same conditions. In the same container, 14.0 g of Cu and 4.0 g of $\mathrm{O_2}$ are reacted until one reactant is used up. Which result is correct?

options.a: $\mathrm{CuO}$ 17.5 g formed, $\mathrm{O_2}$ 0.5 g left over
options.b: $\mathrm{CuO}$ 18.0 g formed, nothing left over
options.c: $\mathrm{CuO}$ 17.5 g formed, Cu 0.5 g left over
options.d: $\mathrm{CuO}$ 20.0 g formed, no $\mathrm{O_2}$ left, Cu left over

hints: In (C), where Cu is in excess, the 10.0 g of CuO contains all 2.0 g of O from the container, so find the Cu:O mass ratio, then check which reactant runs short. Mass of product = Cu reacted + O reacted.
(C): CuO 10.0 g = Cu 8.0 g + O 2.0 g, so Cu:O = 4:1. O needed for 14.0 g Cu is $14.0 \times \frac{1}{4} = 3.5$ g < 4.0 g, so Cu is the limiting reactant.
chemistry-killer-01.explanation:
Step 1: In (C), adding more Cu does not raise CuO above 10.0 g, so all 2.0 g of $\mathrm{O_2}$ reacted: CuO 10.0 g = Cu 8.0 g + O 2.0 g, i.e. Cu:O = 4:1. (Check: in (A) Cu 4.0 g + O 1.0 g = 5.0 g with O left over; in (B) Cu 8.0 g + O 2.0 g = 10.0 g exactly; in (C) 4.0 g Cu is left over.)
Step 2: O needed for 14.0 g Cu = $14.0 \times \frac{1}{4} = 3.5$ g. Since 4.0 g of $\mathrm{O_2}$ is supplied, all the Cu reacts and $4.0-3.5=0.5$ g of $\mathrm{O_2}$ remains.
Step 3: CuO formed = 14.0 + 3.5 = 17.5 g (Cu:O:CuO = 4:1:5).
Answer: a (CuO 17.5 g, $\mathrm{O_2}$ 0.5 g left). (Wrong options: 18.0 g adds the unreacted O; 20.0 g is computed from 4.0 g O ignoring that Cu runs out.)

chemistry-killer-02.prompt:
At constant temperature and pressure, hydrogen ($\mathrm{H_2}$) reacts with oxygen ($\mathrm{O_2}$) to form water vapor ($\mathrm{H_2O}$(g)). Different gas mixtures were reacted completely and the total gas volume was measured at the same temperature and pressure (all water is gaseous).
(A) $\mathrm{H_2}$ 30 mL + $\mathrm{O_2}$ 20 mL -> total 35 mL after reaction
(B) $\mathrm{H_2}$ 20 mL + $\mathrm{O_2}$ 20 mL -> total 30 mL after reaction
A 60 mL mixture of $\mathrm{H_2}$ and $\mathrm{O_2}$ was reacted completely at the same temperature and pressure. The total volume after reaction was 45 mL and the only gas left over was $\mathrm{O_2}$ (no $\mathrm{H_2}$ left). Which pair correctly gives the volume of $\mathrm{H_2}$ before reaction and the volume of $\mathrm{O_2}$ left after reaction, in that order?

options.a: 40 mL, 20 mL
options.b: 30 mL, 15 mL
options.c: 20 mL, 30 mL
options.d: 45 mL, 15 mL

hints: In $\mathrm{2H_2 + O_2 \rightarrow 2H_2O(g)}$, 3 volumes of gas become 2 volumes, so the decrease in volume equals the volume of $\mathrm{O_2}$ that reacted.
Decrease = 60 - 45 = 15 mL = $\mathrm{O_2}$ reacted. All the $\mathrm{H_2}$ reacted, so $\mathrm{H_2}$ = 15 x 2 = 30 mL and $\mathrm{H_2O(g)}$ formed = 30 mL.
chemistry-killer-02.explanation:
Step 1: From (A) and (B) the volume ratio. (B): 20 mL of H2 reacts with 10 mL of O2 to give 20 mL of H2O, 10 mL of O2 left, total 30 mL. (A): 30 mL of H2 reacts with 15 mL of O2 to give 30 mL of H2O, 5 mL of O2 left, total 35 mL. So $\mathrm{H_2:O_2:H_2O(g)} = 2:1:2$.
Step 2: Volume falls from 60 mL to 45 mL, a decrease of 15 mL. Each reaction of 3 volumes into 2 loses 1 volume, equal to the O2 volume reacted, so O2 reacted = 15 mL.
Step 3: No H2 is left, so H2 reacted = 15 x 2 = 30 mL, H2O(g) = 30 mL. Total after = 45 mL, so O2 left = 45 - 30 = 15 mL. Initial O2 = 15 + 15 = 30 mL, and 30 + 30 = 60 mL checks out.
Answer: 30 mL, 15 mL (b).

chemistry-killer-03.prompt: 14 g of nitrogen ($\mathrm{N_2}$) and 4 g of hydrogen ($\mathrm{H_2}$) are reacted completely in a vessel to form ammonia ($\mathrm{NH_3}$). The reaction is $\mathrm{N_2 + 3H_2 \rightarrow 2NH_3}$, with atomic masses H = 1, N = 14, and it proceeds until one reactant is used up. Which pair correctly gives the mass (g) of $\mathrm{NH_3}$ formed and the volume of all gas in the vessel after the reaction, converted to standard temperature and pressure (STP, 1 mol = 22.4 L), in that order?
hints: Find the moles of each substance and compare each divided by its coefficient to find the limiting reactant. Gas after reaction = $\mathrm{NH_3}$ formed + $\mathrm{H_2}$ left.
$\mathrm{N_2}$ = 14/28 = 0.5 mol, $\mathrm{H_2}$ = 4/2 = 2 mol. 0.5/1 = 0.5 < 2/3 ≈ 0.67, so $\mathrm{N_2}$ is limiting and $\mathrm{NH_3}$ = 0.5 x 2 = 1 mol.
chemistry-killer-03.explanation:
Step 1: Moles. $\mathrm{N_2}$ 14 g / 28 g/mol = 0.5 mol; $\mathrm{H_2}$ 4 g / 2 g/mol = 2 mol.
Step 2: Divide by coefficients. $\mathrm{N_2}$: 0.5/1 = 0.5; $\mathrm{H_2}$: 2/3 ≈ 0.67. The smaller value belongs to $\mathrm{N_2}$, the limiting reactant.
Step 3: 0.5 mol $\mathrm{N_2}$ reacts with 1.5 mol $\mathrm{H_2}$ to give 1.0 mol $\mathrm{NH_3}$. Mass = 1.0 x 17 = 17 g. $\mathrm{H_2}$ left = 2 - 1.5 = 0.5 mol.
Step 4: Total gas = 1.0 + 0.5 = 1.5 mol, volume at STP = 1.5 x 22.4 = 33.6 L.
Answer: 17 g, 33.6 L (c). (Wrong options: 22.4 L ignores the leftover H2; 34 g mixes up the mole counts and coefficients; 8.5 g treats N2:NH3 as 1:1.)

chemistry-killer-04.prompt:
At 25 °C, $v$ mL of $\mathrm{HCl(aq)}$ of unknown concentration is added to 50 mL of 1.0 M $\mathrm{NaOH(aq)}$, and the maximum temperature of the mixture is measured. Both solutions are at 20.0 °C before mixing.
Volume of HCl, $v$ (mL): 0 / 10 / 25 / 40 / 50
Maximum temperature after mixing (°C): 20.0 / 24.5 / 29.0 / 27.5 / 26.75
Assume the mixture has density 1.0 g/mL and specific heat 4.0 J/(g·°C), the volumes are additive, and no heat is lost. The reaction is $\mathrm{H^+ + OH^- \rightarrow H_2O}$. Which pair correctly gives the concentration of HCl(aq) and the heat of neutralization (heat released per 1 mol of water formed, kJ/mol), in that order?

options.a: 1.0 M, 54 kJ/mol
options.b: 2.0 M, 36 kJ/mol
options.c: 2.0 M, 108 kJ/mol
options.d: 2.0 M, 54 kJ/mol

hints: The temperature peak is exactly the neutralization point: $M_{\mathrm{HCl}}V_{\mathrm{HCl}} = M_{\mathrm{NaOH}}V_{\mathrm{NaOH}}$. Heat released $Q = mc\Delta T$; heat of neutralization = $Q$ / moles of water formed.
At $v$ = 25 mL: $M \times 25 = 1.0 \times 50$, so M = 2.0 M. Then $Q = (75\,\mathrm{g}) \times 4.0 \times (29.0-20.0) = 2700$ J = 2.7 kJ, forming 0.050 mol of water.
chemistry-killer-04.explanation:
Step 1: The temperature rises with $v$, peaks at 29.0 °C at 25 mL, then falls as unreacted solution accumulates (and the total volume grows). So at 25 mL, H+ and OH- react exactly.
Step 2: NaOH = 1.0 M x 0.050 L = 0.050 mol reacts 1:1 with HCl, so 0.050 mol HCl is in 25 mL: 0.050 / 0.025 = 2.0 M.
Step 3: Q = mc$\Delta$T = (50 + 25 mL x 1.0 g/mL) x 4.0 x 9.0 = 75 x 4.0 x 9.0 = 2700 J.
Step 4: Heat of neutralization = 2700 J / 0.050 mol = 54000 J/mol = 54 kJ/mol.
Check: at $v$ = 10 mL, 0.020 mol H+ reacts, $\Delta$T = 0.020 x 54000 / (60 x 4.0) = 4.5, so 24.5 °C. At 40 mL, 0.050 mol OH- reacts, $\Delta$T = 2700 / (90 x 4.0) = 7.5, so 27.5 °C.
Answer: 2.0 M, 54 kJ/mol (d). (Wrong options: 36 kJ/mol uses a 50 g mass; 108 kJ/mol uses 0.025 mol of water.)

chemistry-killer-05.prompt:
0.1 M $\mathrm{NaOH(aq)}$ is added to 50 mL of 0.2 M $\mathrm{HCl(aq)}$, and the total number of ions (mmol) in the solution is recorded. Water is not counted as ions, and only $\mathrm{H^+ + OH^- \rightarrow H_2O}$ occurs.
Volume of NaOH(aq) added (mL): 0 / 50 / 100
Total ions (mmol): 20 / 20 / 20
When 150 mL of NaOH(aq) has been added, which pair correctly gives the number ratio $\mathrm{Na^+ : Cl^- : OH^-}$ in the mixture and (total ions after mixing) / (total ions originally in the 50 mL of HCl(aq) plus the 150 mL of NaOH(aq)), in that order? (Ignore autoionization of water.)
hints: Net ions ($\mathrm{H^+}$, $\mathrm{OH^-}$) are consumed 1:1 to form water, while spectator ions ($\mathrm{Na^+}$, $\mathrm{Cl^-}$) keep their numbers. Number of ions = concentration x volume (mmol).
HCl 50 mL: $\mathrm{H^+}$ = $\mathrm{Cl^-}$ = 10 mmol. NaOH 150 mL: $\mathrm{Na^+}$ = $\mathrm{OH^-}$ = 15 mmol. $\mathrm{OH^-}$ left = 15 - 10 = 5 mmol.
chemistry-killer-05.explanation:
Step 1: Reading the table. 0 mL: H+ 10 + Cl- 10 = 20. 50 mL: H+ 5, Cl- 10, Na+ 5 = 20. 100 mL: Cl- 10, Na+ 10 = 20 (neutralization point). Up to that point each H+ is replaced by a Na+, so the total stays constant.
Step 2: At 150 mL the NaOH supplies Na+ 15 mmol and OH- 15 mmol. 10 mmol of OH- reacts with the 10 mmol of H+, leaving OH- 5 mmol. Ions: Na+ 15, Cl- 10, OH- 5, ratio 3 : 2 : 1, total 30 mmol.
Step 3: Ions before mixing = (10 + 10) + (15 + 15) = 50 mmol. Ratio = 30/50 = 3/5.
Answer: 3 : 2 : 1, 3/5 (a). (Wrong options: OH- = 15 ignores neutralization; 5/3 inverts the ratio; 3/4 miscounts the ions before mixing as 40.)

chemistry-killer-06.prompt:
The colour-change ranges of indicators are:
Methyl orange: red at pH < 3.1, orange at 3.1 to 4.4, yellow at pH > 4.4
BTB: yellow at pH < 6.0, green at 6.0 to 7.6, blue at pH > 7.6
Phenolphthalein: colourless at pH < 8.3, pink at 8.3 to 10.0, red at pH > 10.0
Three everyday aqueous solutions were tested with all three indicators.
(A) Stomach-acid model solution: methyl orange red, BTB yellow, phenolphthalein colourless
(B) Solution after an antacid was added and fully reacted: methyl orange yellow, BTB yellow, phenolphthalein colourless
(C) Dilute sodium hydrogencarbonate solution: methyl orange yellow, BTB blue, phenolphthalein colourless
If the pH range satisfying all three indicator results is narrowed down as far as possible, which option correctly gives the pH ranges of (A), (B), (C) in order?
hints: Take the intersection (common part) of the pH ranges given by each indicator result.

(A): methyl orange red gives pH < 3.1, which already satisfies BTB yellow (pH < 6.0) and phenolphthalein colourless (pH < 8.3), so pH < 3.1. (B): methyl orange yellow pH > 4.4 and BTB yellow pH < 6.0 give 4.4 < pH < 6.0.
chemistry-killer-06.explanation:
(A): methyl orange red pH < 3.1, BTB yellow pH < 6.0, phenolphthalein colourless pH < 8.3. Common range: pH < 3.1.
(B): methyl orange yellow pH > 4.4, BTB yellow pH < 6.0, phenolphthalein colourless pH < 8.3. Common range: 4.4 < pH < 6.0.
(C): methyl orange yellow pH > 4.4, BTB blue pH > 7.6, phenolphthalein colourless pH < 8.3. Common range: 7.6 < pH < 8.3.
Answer: (A) pH < 3.1, (B) 4.4 < pH < 6.0, (C) 7.6 < pH < 8.3 (b). (Wrong options: reading (A) as 3.1 to 4.4 confuses red with orange; reading (B) as 6.0 to 7.6 confuses BTB yellow with green; the last option uses only the BTB range and is not the narrowest.)

chemistry-killer-07.prompt: At standard temperature and pressure (STP, 0 °C, 1 atm; 1 mol of gas = 22.4 L), a gas mixture of methane ($\mathrm{CH_4}$) and carbon dioxide ($\mathrm{CO_2}$) has a volume of 11.2 L and a mass of 16.4 g. Atomic masses are H = 1, C = 12, O = 16, and Avogadro's number is $N_A$. How many atoms in total are in this mixture?
hints: Use total moles $n = V/22.4$ and the mass equation $16x + 44y = 16.4$ (x, y = moles of $\mathrm{CH_4}$, $\mathrm{CO_2}$). Atoms = (atoms per molecule) x moles x $N_A$.
chemistry-killer-07.explanation:
Step 1: Total moles = 11.2 L / 22.4 L/mol = 0.5 mol, so x + y = 0.5.
Step 2: Mass: 16x + 44y = 16.4. Substitute y = 0.5 - x: 16x + 22 - 44x = 16.4, so 28x = 5.6, x = 0.2, y = 0.3.
Step 3: Atoms: $\mathrm{CH_4}$ has 5 atoms per molecule, 0.2 x 5 = 1.0 mol; $\mathrm{CO_2}$ has 3, 0.3 x 3 = 0.9 mol. Total 1.9 mol of atoms = $1.9\,N_A$.
Answer: $1.9\,N_A$ (c). (Wrong options: 1.5 assumes all CO2, 2.5 assumes all CH4, 1.7 counts only 4 atoms for CH4.)

chemistry-killer-08.prompt: A 20 % (by mass) aqueous sodium hydroxide solution ($\mathrm{NaOH}$, formula mass 40) has a density of 1.2 g/mL. It is diluted with water to prepare 600 mL of 0.5 M NaOH(aq). What volume (mL) of the 20 % NaOH solution is needed? (Atomic masses H = 1, O = 16, Na = 23. Molarity $M = \frac{10xd}{M_w}$, where x is the mass percent and d is the solution density in g/mL.)

options.a: 60 mL
options.b: 5.0 mL
options.c: 72 mL
options.d: 50 mL

hints: Find the molarity of the 20 % solution with $M = \frac{10xd}{M_w}$, then use conservation of moles of solute on dilution ($M_1V_1 = M_2V_2$).
chemistry-killer-08.explanation:
Step 1: Molarity of 20 % NaOH: $M = \frac{10 \times 20 \times 1.2}{40} = 6.0$ mol/L (1 L = 1200 g of solution containing 240 g NaOH = 6 mol).
Step 2: Solute in the target solution = 0.5 mol/L x 0.600 L = 0.30 mol (12 g NaOH).
Step 3: Moles of solute are unchanged on dilution: 6.0 x V = 0.30, V = 0.050 L = 50 mL. (Check: 12 g / 0.20 = 60 g of solution, 60 g / 1.2 g/mL = 50 mL.)
Answer: 50 mL (d). (Wrong options: 60 mL ignores density, giving M = 5.0; 72 mL multiplies 60 g by the density; 5.0 mL is a decimal-place error.)

chemistry-killer-09.prompt: At constant temperature and pressure, gases A and B react to form gas C in $\mathrm{aA(g) + bB(g) \rightarrow cC(g)}$. 20 mL of A and 60 mL of B react exactly to give 40 mL of C. The molecular mass of A is 28 and that of B is 2. A 100 mL mixture of A and B (average molecular mass 12.4) is reacted completely at the same temperature and pressure. How many times the density of the gas mixture before the reaction is the density of the gas mixture after the reaction?
hints: At the same temperature and pressure, gas density is proportional to average molecular mass, and mass is conserved, so the density ratio is the inverse of the volume ratio. Use the average molecular mass to find the volumes of A and B.
28x + 2(100 - x) = 12.4 x 100 gives x = 40 mL (A) and B = 60 mL. With A:B:C = 1:3:2, all 60 mL of B reacts using 20 mL of A and forming 40 mL of C, leaving 20 mL of A, so the total after is 60 mL.
chemistry-killer-09.explanation:
Step 1: Volume ratio A:B:C = 20:60:40 = 1:3:2, i.e. $\mathrm{A + 3B \rightarrow 2C}$.
Step 2: In the 100 mL mixture let A = x mL: (28x + 2(100 - x))/100 = 12.4, so 26x + 200 = 1240 and x = 40 mL. A = 40 mL, B = 60 mL.
Step 3: All 60 mL of B reacts, using 20 mL of A and giving 40 mL of C. After the reaction: A 20 mL + C 40 mL = 60 mL.
Step 4: Mass is conserved (check: before 40 x 28 + 60 x 2 = 1240; C has molecular mass (28 + 3 x 2)/2 = 17, after 20 x 28 + 40 x 17 = 1240). At the same T and P, density = mass/volume, so after/before = 100/60 = 5/3.
Answer: 5/3 (a). (Wrong options: 3/5 inverts the ratio; 1 uses mass conservation but ignores the volume change; 5/4 wrongly leaves 40 mL of A, giving a total of 80 mL.)

chemistry-killer-10.prompt:
Consider the ammonia-synthesis equilibrium $\mathrm{N_2(g) + 3H_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2NH_3(g)}$, $\Delta H < 0$ (exothermic). Starting from equilibrium in a sealed vessel at constant temperature, each of the following changes is made separately and a new equilibrium is reached.
(A) Keeping the temperature constant, the volume of the vessel is decreased.
(B) Keeping the volume constant, the temperature is raised.
(C) Keeping temperature and volume constant, unreactive Ar(g) is added.
(D) Keeping temperature and total pressure constant, Ar(g) is added so that the volume increases.
(E) Keeping temperature and volume constant, $\mathrm{H_2(g)}$ is added.
Select all the cases in which the amount (mol) of $\mathrm{NH_3}$ at the new equilibrium is greater than at the original equilibrium.
hints: Le Chatelier's principle: the equilibrium shifts to reduce the change. Moles of gas go 4 -> 2, and the forward reaction is exothermic.

(A) pressure up: shifts to fewer moles (forward). (B) temperature up: shifts to the endothermic side (reverse). (C) constant V, Ar added: no concentration change, no shift. (D) constant P, Ar added: volume grows (partial pressures fall), shifts to more moles (reverse). (E) $\mathrm{H_2}$ added: forward.
chemistry-killer-10.explanation:
Step 1: Gas moles go from 4 (reactants) to 2 (product). The forward reaction is exothermic.
Step 2: (A) Decreasing volume raises pressure, so the equilibrium shifts toward fewer gas moles (forward) and NH3 increases.
(B) Raising temperature favours the endothermic reverse reaction, so NH3 decreases.
(C) At constant volume, adding Ar leaves the concentrations (partial pressures) of N2, H2, NH3 unchanged, so Q = K and nothing shifts; NH3 is unchanged.
(D) At constant pressure, adding Ar expands the volume and lowers all reactant and product concentrations, so the equilibrium shifts to the side with more gas moles (reverse) and NH3 decreases.
(E) Adding H2 makes Q < K, so the forward reaction proceeds and the amount of NH3 (mol) increases.
Step 3: NH3 increases in (A) and (E).
Answer: (A), (E) (b).

chemistry-killer-11.prompt:
For $\mathrm{N_2O_4(g) \rightleftharpoons 2NO_2(g)}$, the equilibrium constant in concentrations is $K = 0.4$ (units omitted) at a certain temperature. At this temperature, $\mathrm{N_2O_4}$ and $\mathrm{NO_2}$ are placed in three vessels and left for a long time.
(A) Volume 2.0 L, $\mathrm{N_2O_4}$ 0.4 mol, $\mathrm{NO_2}$ 0.4 mol
(B) Volume 0.5 L, $\mathrm{N_2O_4}$ 0.1 mol, $\mathrm{NO_2}$ 0.2 mol
(C) Volume 2.0 L, $\mathrm{N_2O_4}$ 0.2 mol, $\mathrm{NO_2}$ 0.4 mol
Comparing the reaction quotient $Q$ with $K$, which option correctly gives the direction of net reaction in each vessel on the way to equilibrium?

options.a: (A) at equilibrium, (B) at equilibrium, (C) reverse reaction
options.b: (A) forward reaction, (B) forward reaction, (C) at equilibrium
options.c: (A) forward reaction, (B) reverse reaction, (C) at equilibrium
options.d: (A) reverse reaction, (B) forward reaction, (C) at equilibrium

hints: Substitute molar concentrations (mol/L, not moles) into $Q = \frac{[\mathrm{NO_2}]^2}{[\mathrm{N_2O_4}]}$. Q < K: forward; Q > K: reverse; Q = K: equilibrium.
chemistry-killer-11.explanation:
Step 1: Concentrations. (A) 2.0 L: [N2O4] = 0.4/2.0 = 0.2 M, [NO2] = 0.2 M. (B) 0.5 L: [N2O4] = 0.1/0.5 = 0.2 M, [NO2] = 0.2/0.5 = 0.4 M. (C) 2.0 L: [N2O4] = 0.1 M, [NO2] = 0.2 M.
Step 2: Q. (A) Q = 0.2^2/0.2 = 0.2 < 0.4, forward. (B) Q = 0.4^2/0.2 = 0.8 > 0.4, reverse. (C) Q = 0.2^2/0.1 = 0.4 = K, equilibrium.
Answer: (A) forward, (B) reverse, (C) equilibrium (c). (Wrong options: using moles instead of concentrations gives Q = 0.4^2/0.4 = 0.4 for (A) and 0.2^2/0.1 = 0.4 for (B), so both look like equilibrium.)

chemistry-killer-12.prompt: At 25 °C the $\mathrm{p}K_a$ of acetic acid ($\mathrm{CH_3COOH}$) is 4.7. A buffer is made by mixing 100 mL of 0.20 M $\mathrm{CH_3COOH}$ with 100 mL of 0.10 M $\mathrm{CH_3COONa}$. Then 10 mL of 1.0 M $\mathrm{NaOH(aq)}$ is added. What is the pH of the solution? (Changes in concentration due to volume change do not affect the ratio calculation; use $\log 2 = 0.30$. The NaOH reacts completely with acetic acid.)
hints: Use the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation $\mathrm{pH = p}K_a + \log\frac{[\mathrm{A^-}]}{[\mathrm{HA}]}$ after first finding the change in moles from $\mathrm{OH^- + HA \rightarrow A^- + H_2O}$.
Initially HA = 0.20 x 0.100 = 20 mmol and A⁻ = 0.10 x 0.100 = 10 mmol. Adding 10 mmol NaOH gives HA = 10 mmol and A⁻ = 20 mmol, so [A⁻]/[HA] = 2.
chemistry-killer-12.explanation:
Step 1: Initial moles: HA = 20 mmol, A⁻ = 10 mmol (initial pH = 4.7 + log 0.5 = 4.7 - 0.30 = 4.4).
Step 2: NaOH = 1.0 M x 10 mL = 10 mmol. In $\mathrm{OH^- + HA \rightarrow A^- + H_2O}$, HA falls by 10 mmol and A⁻ rises by 10 mmol: HA = 10 mmol, A⁻ = 20 mmol.
Step 3: Both are in the same solution, so the concentration ratio equals the mole ratio = 2. pH = 4.7 + log 2 = 4.7 + 0.30 = 5.0.
Answer: 5.0 (d). (Wrong options: 4.4 is the pH before NaOH was added; 4.7 wrongly takes HA = A⁻; 5.3 uses a ratio of 4.)
